title: How Morphic Fields Work?
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant, with guest producer Dylan, examine biologist Rupert Sheldrake and his hypothesis of morphic fields and morphic resonance, which he proposes guide the development of living things and pass learned behavior across generations. They cover his scientific training, his 1981 book A New Science of Life, the scientific establishment's harsh reaction (including Sir John Maddox's "best candidate for burning" editorial in Nature), and tests of his ideas: the dog Jaytee who waits at the window for owner Pam, lab rat maze learning across generations, and chick experiments with Steven Rose. They also discuss skeptic Richard Wiseman's replication, Sheldrake's later books such as The Science Delusion, his TEDx talk on changing constants, and his critiques of scientific dogma. The episode closes with a listener mail from a University of Iowa student about the 2020 Iowa caucus.

segments.title: Opening banter and tour plugs
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with tour dates in Vancouver and Portland, then Josh introduces the episode on Rupert Sheldrake, noting the hosts are tired from a rescheduled recording.
topics: Stuff You Should Know live tour

segments.title: Who is Rupert Sheldrake
segments.summary: The hosts describe Sheldrake as a heretic in the scientific community who is nonetheless trained as a scientist, with degrees and a Royal Society post in plant biology, and who is polite and engages critics.

segments.title: Morphogenesis and the origins of morphic fields
segments.summary: The hosts explain the unanswered question of how organisms take their shape, and trace the 1920s-30s idea of morphogenetic fields through C. H. Waddington and Alexander Gurwitsch.

segments.title: Morphic resonance explained
segments.summary: Sheldrake's 1981 book A New Science of Life proposes that morphic fields guide form and behavior, with morphic resonance passing memory across space and time. Sheldrake's definition is quoted and the idea that laws of nature are habits is raised.

segments.title: Questions about similarity and animal behavior examples
segments.summary: The hosts question what similarity triggers morphic resonance and list examples Sheldrake cites, such as fish schooling, monarch migration, homing pigeons, termite nests, and dogs anticipating owners. They discuss human peripheral vision and snake detection.

segments.title: Human examples: crosswords and being stared at
segments.summary: Sheldrake's claims that crossword puzzles are easier later in the day and that people can sense being stared at are discussed, with the hosts offering a simpler explanation for the staring effect.

segments.title: Scientific reaction and Sir John Maddox
segments.summary: The hosts describe the backlash, including Sir John Maddox's Nature editorial calling A New Science of Life a candidate for burning, and other critics such as Lewis Wolpert calling it junk. Sheldrake's response defends falsifiability.

segments.title: Experiments: Jaytee the dog and the Wiseman replication
segments.summary: Sheldrake's experiments on Pam's dog Jaytee, which reportedly anticipated her return home, are described. Richard Wiseman's replication found the dog responded before the ten-minute window, and Sheldrake's rebuttal is outlined.

segments.title: Lab rats, chicks, and critics' views
segments.summary: The hosts describe lab rat maze experiments showing improvement across generations and Steven Rose's chick experiments. They discuss Rose's criticism that Sheldrake is unlikely to accept disconfirmation, Sheldrake's claims about dogma, and his critique of the Big Bang.

segments.title: Sheldrake's later books, TEDx talk and the hosts' takeaways
segments.summary: The hosts discuss The Science Delusion, Sheldrake's TEDx talk about possibly changing constants of nature, a comparison to pseudoscience that they call unfair, and their conclusion that listeners should make up their own minds.

segments.title: Listener mail: Iowa caucus
segments.summary: Lauren, a University of Iowa student, describes crowding, long lines, and a two-and-a-half-hour counting process at her Iowa caucus site in Iowa City, and predicts the caucus system will eventually end.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and close the episode with contact information.
